comparison: Both strongly support the core finding of functional hierarchy through optogenetic perturbation (C49-C54, C93, C105). OpenEval emphasizes statistical robustness (p=0.012, p=0.021) and consistent effects across neurons. Peer reviewers unanimously affirm this as 'convincing evidence' with appropriate timescales ruling out feedback artifacts. This represents the central experimental finding with full agreement.

Both support that motor cortical regions rapidly influence muscle activity (C39-C42). OpenEval highlights strong statistical evidence (p<10^-10) and rapid timescales (25-100ms) supporting oligosynaptic influence. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as part of the causal evidence for hierarchical interaction, with no challenges raised.

Both support earlier RFA activity (C43-C48). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of multiple analytical approaches (activity state deviation, onset times, variance fractions) with consistent statistics. Peer Reviewer 4 acknowledges the finding but notes it 'calls into question previous interpretations of earlier rising activity in PM as reflecting a hierarchy mediated by feedforward influence,' suggesting the interpretation differs from traditional views.

Both address methodological aspects (C43-C44 in overlap with C34-C38). OpenEval R3 focuses on establishing earlier RFA activity through multiple analyses. Peer R9 acknowledges the experimental methods and dataset quality without challenge. Minimal overlap in specific claims but both support the experimental foundation.

Both address high similarity between regions using CCA and PLS (C55-C60, C95). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative metrics (92% and 98% variance capture) as strong evidence. Peer reviewers accept the findings but raise methodological concerns about trial-averaging potentially inflating perceived similarities. The finding is not disputed, but its interpretation is questioned.

Perfect claim overlap (C61-C63) on maximal alignment at zero lag. OpenEval treats this as supported evidence important for interpreting hierarchy-firing pattern relationships. Peer Reviewer 2 expresses confusion about why shifting doesn't change outcomes and finds 'interpretation remains ambiguous,' indicating uncertainty about what this result means for the claimed hierarchy.

Both address asymmetry in lagged activity patterns using DLAG (C64-C69, C94). OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance (p=0.021) and consistency across metrics as supporting hierarchy at population level. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as evidence of asymmetry with RFA leading CFA, but note it contrasts with other analyses showing no asymmetry, highlighting the complexity of the findings.

Both address symmetric predictivity using multiple methods (C70-C82, C96). OpenEval emphasizes consistency across three independent methods (Granger, transfer entropy, CCM) as key finding showing dissociation between functional influence and firing pattern predictivity. Peer reviewers fully accept these findings and note 'no asymmetry was observed...with methods computed on individual neuron pairs,' treating this as important evidence of complexity.

Both address computational modeling showing hierarchy can emerge from local dynamics differences (C86-C92, C97, C131, C133). OpenEval emphasizes model fit quality and striking finding that actual input was larger CFA→RFA despite opposite influence dominance. Peer reviewers acknowledge modeling positively as 'important demonstration,' but Reviewer 4 cautions that local circuit dynamics centrality 'is not supported by experimental data' and only by the model.

Both address the main conclusion integrating all findings (C10, C98-C99, C114, C123, C126, C134). OpenEval treats this as well-justified by convergent evidence from optogenetics, similarity, symmetric predictivity, and modeling. Peer reviewers strongly support this as a key contribution, emphasizing the lesson about limitations of inferring hierarchy from firing patterns alone and the need for caution in interpretation.

Partial overlap on methodological implications (C115, C127-C128). OpenEval R14 focuses on concerns about network modeling and recommendations for anatomically realistic constraints. Peer R8 emphasizes the broader lesson about caution when interpreting inter-regional interactions from neural activity patterns alone. Both support the methodological implications but with different emphases.

Perfect claim overlap (C119-C122) on limitations and alternative interpretations. Both support the authors' cautious interpretation. OpenEval notes this demonstrates 'appropriate scientific restraint.' Peer reviewers appreciate the caution and request more elaboration on why different methods yield different results, suggesting the authors' careful approach is appropriate and valued.

Both address behavioral task and measurement methods (C34-C38). OpenEval emphasizes clear documentation with supporting figures and appropriate citations. Peer reviewers acknowledge the 'valuable dataset' and experimental methods without challenge. Full agreement on methodological foundation.
